- Tell the server immediately and clearly: “I am highly allergic to peanuts. This is life‑threatening for me. Can you notify the chef/manager right now?”
- Ask specific questions:
  - “Do you have a written allergen policy? Do you prepare peanuts on the premises?”
  - “Which dishes contain peanuts or peanut oil, or are made in the same area as peanuts?”
  - “Can the kitchen prepare [dish name] in a clean area with new gloves, clean utensils and a clean pan? Will they avoid garnishes/peanut sauces?”

- Any item listing peanuts, peanut sauce, peanut oil, groundnut, satay, or “peanut brittle,” “peanut butter,” etc.

- “Please tell the cook to wash hands, change gloves, and use a clean pan/utensils for this order. No garnishes or sauces that aren’t verified peanut‑free.”
- “Please serve the food on a clean plate, not a plate used for other orders.”

- If you do not have epinephrine and symptoms suggest systemic reaction, call emergency services immediately.

- Keep the restaurant manager informed and document what you were served; take a photo of the plate/packaging and any labels if available.
- Save any remaining food for testing if needed and inform your clinician.
- Review the event with your clinician to decide if changes in your emergency plan or prescriptions are needed.

- Carry a printed allergy card you can hand to staff (one sentence: “I am highly allergic to peanuts. Any cross‑contact may be life‑threatening. Please check with the kitchen.”).
- Prefer restaurants that offer sealed, packaged desserts or that will prepare simple dishes from scratch on request.

answer:
Short answer — for the sharpest, most comfortable distance vision get single‑vision distance lenses that match your current prescription, plus these lens choices and coatings:

1. Lens type
- Single‑vision distance lenses (unless you need near reading correction or have presbyopia — then discuss progressives or bifocals with your fitter).  
- Aspheric or atoric design: flattens the lens surface and improves peripheral clarity and cosmetic appearance, especially helpful with moderate‑to‑high myopia.

2. Lens material / index (choose by prescription strength and desired thinness)
- Mild prescriptions (~–1.00 to –3.00): 1.59 (polycarbonate or 1.56) or standard plastic (CR‑39) is OK.  
- Moderate (~–3.00 to –6.00): 1.67 high‑index is a good balance of thinness and cost.  
- Strong (≈ –6.00 and stronger): 1.74 high‑index gives the thinnest, lightest lenses.  
- If you need impact resistance (sports, certain jobs) choose polycarbonate or Trivex.

3. Coatings and treatments (most important for comfort/sharpness)
- Anti‑reflective (multilayer AR): biggest single improvement for perceived sharpness, reduces reflections and night‑time glare.  
- Scratch‑resistant hard coat (standard and needed).  
- Oleophobic/ hydrophobic and anti‑smudge top coat: keeps lenses clearer and easier to clean.  
- UV protection (UV400): blocks harmful UV even in clear lenses.  
- Blue‑light filtering: optional — won’t improve sharpness but may reduce perceived glare or sleep‑disrupting blue at night if you want it.  
- Photochromic (Transitions): convenient if you want one pair for indoor/outdoor, but consider separate polarized sunglasses for driving (Transitions are slower in cars because windshields block the UV that activates them).

4. Fit and measurements
- Have an up‑to‑date prescription and an accurate pupillary distance (PD).  
- Make sure the optical centers of the lenses line up with your pupils and the frame sits at the right height — correct fit matters as much as lens choice for comfortable distance vision.

5. Night / driving considerations
- AR coating plus a higher‑quality aspheric design helps reduce halos and improve contrast at night.  
- For daytime driving, polarized sunglasses are best for glare; for night driving avoid yellow “anti‑glare” tints — stick with AR.

How to decide (quick checklist)
- Do you need distance correction to enjoy/participate? If you can’t comfortably see underwater without correction, pay for the diopter mask. It’s the simplest, safest option.

- What prescription range (diopters) do their masks cover? Do they correct astigmatism?

- Can I try the mask on land before the trip starts?
- Do you allow/use daily disposable contacts if I bring my own (if I prefer contacts)?

- If you need reliable distance vision and want to avoid contacts in seawater, reserve the custom-diopter mask ($40) — it’s inexpensive insurance for an enjoyable trip.
- If your vision is fine unaided or your prescription isn’t supported by diopter masks (or you’re comfortable using daily disposables in the water), skip it.

answer:
Great — here’s a compact, practical set of caption + audio settings you can try to make movie nights easier, based on your need for captions and wanting clearer dialogue without mangling the rest of the soundtrack.

Captions / subtitles (visual settings)
- Use SDH/CC (Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard-of-hearing) if available — they include speaker IDs and sound cues.
- Font: clean sans-serif (e.g., Arial, Helvetica, Open Sans). Avoid ornate or condensed fonts.
- Size: large enough to read from your seating position — many TVs/devices let you pick Normal/Large/Extra Large; start at Large. If the device uses percentages, try ~130–160%.
- Color & contrast: white or off-white text with a thick black outline (stroke) OR a semi-opaque black background box. This keeps text readable over bright/dark scenes.
- Background opacity: ~50–70% if using a box; prefer a background box when the image is busy.
- Lines/placement: limit to 2 lines max, centered at the bottom. Keep margins slightly inset from the screen edge.
- Styling: disable italics for general text unless the app uses italics only for off‑screen or non‑spoken sounds. Increase caption display time or reading speed if your device allows (longer dwell helps comprehension).
- System-wide: set captions at the OS/TV level so they apply across apps (Netflix, Prime, etc.) rather than customizing per app.

Audio hardware & modes (high-level)
- Best option: AVR + dedicated center speaker. That anchors voices and gives precise level control.
- If you keep a soundbar: choose one with a real center driver (not only virtual dialogue mode). Use its “speech”/“dialogue” mode if it’s subtle.
- Turn off aggressive post-processing/surround virtualization on the TV if it moves voices off-center or smears clarity.

Specific audio settings to try (start here and tweak)
- Center channel level: raise the center +2 to +4 dB relative to left/right to make vocals sit forward without sounding separate from the scene.
- Dynamic range: enable light/low dynamic range compression or “volume leveling” (not max/night mode). This reduces loud jumps but avoids flattening. If there’s a choice, pick “Light” or “Medium,” avoid “Max”/“Night” which over-compresses.
- Dialogue enhancement: turn on a mild dialogue enhancement if available, but switch it off if voices start to sound nasal/echo-y.
- EQ (gentle, targeted): boost the presence band and reduce muddiness:
  - +2 to +4 dB around 1.5–3 kHz (where speech clarity resides)
  - -1 to -4 dB around 200–500 Hz to reduce chestiness/mud that can mask consonants
  - Keep bass/subwoofer slightly lower if it’s masking speech (try reducing sub by 2–4 dB)
- Automatic room calibration: run Audyssey/YPAO/Dirac if your AVR/soundbar has it, then manually nudge the center +2–3 dB and make the EQ tweaks above.
- Lip sync: ensure audio delay/lip‑sync is correct so captions match the speech.
- Surrounds: don’t over-raise surround levels — that can pull focus from the center talker.

Practical step-by-step tuning
1. Turn on SDH/CC captions and set the visual style (large, white with black outline or box).
2. Play a dialogue-heavy scene with background music/noise.
3. Run automatic room calibration if available.
4. Raise the center channel +2 dB. Play again; if still hard to follow, go to +3–4 dB.
5. Turn on light dynamic range compression/volume leveling and test. If music/effects sound squashed, back it down.
6. Apply mild EQ: +2–3 dB at ~2 kHz, -2 dB at ~300 Hz. Re-evaluate.
7. If spacing/reading time for captions is short, increase caption display duration or font size.

Extras that help
- Use wireless TV headphones (or stream to hearing aids) for direct, clearer voice delivery while keeping captions on.
- Keep the listening area quiet and reduce reflective hard surfaces (soft furnishings help intelligibility).
- Keep captions enabled even after tuning — they’re the most reliable aid.
- If you watch streaming apps, check each app for caption style options — some let you adjust size and background independently.

answer:
Universal red flags (always get urgent help): sudden severe pain, trouble breathing, chest pain, confusion, fainting, or any symptom that rapidly worsens.

Quick self-care steps to follow right away
- Rest and prioritize sleep (keep your usual wind‑down: book/stretch, avoid screens).
- Hydrate frequently; sip small amounts if nauseous.
- Use simple OTC measures for comfort (fever reducers, analgesics) as you normally would.
- Track key details (time symptoms started, highest temp, vomiting/diarrhea frequency, worsening signs) in your pocket notebook or set a phone reminder to reassess.
- Reassess daily — you want gradual improvement within a few days; if not, escalate.

By condition — what’s OK to wait out vs when to call/seek care

Colds
- OK to wait: congestion/sore throat/mild cough that’s slowly improving and follows the usual pattern; improvement expected by day 3–5.
- Call doctor: symptoms not improving by day 7, or new fever after initial improvement.
- Urgent: universal red flags, or fever >103°F.

Fever
- OK to manage at home: fever under 102°F that lasts less than 3 days and responds to rest/fluids/meds.
- Call doctor: fever 102–103°F lasting more than 3 days, or fever that keeps returning after seeming better.
- Urgent: fever >103°F, or fever with severe headache or stiff neck.

Headache
- OK to wait: a headache like your usual pattern that eases in a few hours with rest/fluids/meds.
- Call doctor: headache lasting >2 days without improvement, or one that’s different from your usual headaches.
- Urgent: sudden “worst ever” headache or any headache with vision change, weakness, trouble speaking, confusion, fainting, or other neurologic signs.

Stomach bug (nausea/vomiting/diarrhea)
- OK to wait: vomiting/diarrhea that improves within 24–48 hours and you can keep small sips of fluid down.
- Call doctor: symptoms lasting 48–72 hours, signs of mild dehydration (darker urine, dizziness), or inability to keep liquids down for ~12 hours.
- Urgent: very little urine, fainting/dizziness, blood in vomit or stool, or severe abdominal pain.

Minor muscle strains
- OK to wait: soreness after activity that gradually improves over 3–5 days; gentle movement as tolerated.
- Call doctor: pain or swelling that isn’t improving after ~1 week, or swelling that keeps getting worse.
- Urgent: can’t bear weight after an injury, severe swelling, numbness or tingling in the limb.

If you’re unsure: follow the universal red flags and seek care. Otherwise, use rest, fluids, simple comfort measures, daily symptom tracking, and a planned reassessment (48–72 hours) to decide whether to call your doctor.

One‑minute self‑care plan (carry this in your pocket)

Immediate steps (first hour)

Home care (0–72 hours)
- Rest, hydrate, light food as tolerated, avoid heavy exertion.

- For muscle strain: gentle movement, ice first 48h, then heat as it improves.

Monitoring timeline & concrete cutoffs
- Universal red flags (go to ER): sudden severe pain, trouble breathing, chest pain, sudden confusion, fainting, severe weakness, slurred speech.  
- Fever: under 102°F and improving within 72 hours → home care. 102–103°F longer than 3 days or recurring → call doctor. Over 103°F or not responding to meds → urgent care/ER.  
- Headache: usual pattern and improves in hours → wait. Lasts >2 days or is different → call doctor. Sudden “worst ever,” vision change, weakness, confusion → urgent care/ER.  
- Vomiting/diarrhea: improves within 24–48 hours and you keep fluids → home. Lasts >48–72 hours or can’t keep liquids for 12 hours or signs of dehydration (dizzy, very little urine) → call doctor. Severe abdominal pain or blood in vomit/stool → urgent care/ER.  
- Cuts: stops with pressure and looks clean → home. Wound edges not closing or spreading redness after a day or two → call doctor. Bleeding that won’t stop after 10 minutes → urgent care/ER.  
- Burns: small red burn improving → home. Large blisters (>quarter), worsening pain after a day → call doctor. Large/deep burns or face/hands/genitals or white/charred skin → urgent care/ER.  
- Back/sciatica: improves over 3–5 days with activity → home. Not improved after 1 week or interfering with sleep → call doctor. New leg weakness, loss of bowel/bladder control, or groin numbness → urgent care/ER.

Nightly 1‑minute routine (combine with your notebook habit)
- Flip quickly to marked pages, confirm whether symptoms improved, unchanged, or worse.

- If any red flag appears, act immediately.

If unsure
- Use telehealth or nurse advice line same day; when in doubt and something feels wrong, get help sooner.

Below is a practical, day‑by‑day two‑week plan you can drop into your schedule. It assumes a focused 4–6 hour editing day and that you’re finishing the “final chapters” (I used six chapters as an example). If you have more/fewer chapters, scale each chapter day proportionally. Throughout, use “one moving part at a time” (fix one kind of problem per pass) and use explicit “zoom out / zoom in” transitions between and within chapters.

Quick setup (Day 0 or morning of Day 1)
- Prepare: open files in Track Changes; make (or refresh) a style sheet with items you must enforce (formatting of gene/protein names, units, serial comma, heading levels, cross‑ref format).
- Create an Author Queries / Issues log (spreadsheet or doc) to collect questions you’ll send to authors.
- Decide daily work blocks (e.g., 2 × 2–3 hour sessions) and schedule quick end‑of‑day checks (15–30 min).

Two‑week schedule

Day 1 — End‑to‑end reading + chapter map
- Do a fast read of all final chapters (no line edits). Note big gaps, duplications, tone/level issues, and where chapter-to-chapter flow feels weak.
- Produce a chapter map: one‑sentence purpose for each chapter and the prerequisite knowledge they require.
Quality checks: each chapter has a one‑line purpose; list of major editorial issues for each chapter.

Day 2 — Macro flow & interchapter transitions
- Fix chapter ordering problems, major reorganizations, and bridging material between chapters.
- Add or rewrite brief “zoom‑out” chapter openings and “zoom‑in” closing paragraphs that explicitly link chapters.
Quality checks: sequential logic holds across chapters; each chapter begins with a contextualizing sentence and ends with a link/preview.

Day 3 — Structural consistency (headings, figures, boxes)
- Normalize heading levels and section ordering. Ensure learning objectives, summaries, or key points are present where required.
- Inventory all figures/tables/boxes and note missing captions, permissions status, and whether each is referenced in text.
Quality checks: heading hierarchy consistent; figure/table inventory completed with permission status.

Days 4–9 — Chapter by chapter detailed passes (one chapter per day)
- Per chapter workflow (do only one “moving part” at a time):
  1. Section/topic sentences pass: ensure every section has a clear topic sentence and that sections flow.
  2. Paragraph clarity pass: rewrite dense paragraphs using “one idea per paragraph”; apply your light metaphors/transitions (zoom in/out) where helpful.
  3. Evidence/accuracy pass: check claims, data statements, units, numbers, and citations for key facts. Flag anything needing author confirmation.
  4. Figures/tables integration pass (if relevant): confirm each figure is placed near first mention; captions state the main takeaway.
- Example allocation if 6 chapters: Day 4 = Chapter A, Day 5 = B, Day 6 = C, Day 7 = D, Day 8 = E, Day 9 = F.
Quality checks per chapter:
  - Topic sentences present and clear.
  - Average paragraph focused on one core idea; no run‑on chains of ideas.
  - Transitions (zoom out/zoom in) at top/bottom of important sections.
  - Key claims have citations or are flagged for citation.

Day 10 — Cross‑chapter consistency and pedagogical elements
- Run a consistency pass: terms, abbreviations, gene/protein formatting, units, notation, box/callout styles.
- Ensure pedagogical elements are present and consistent: summaries, study questions, learning objectives, key terms.
Quality checks: glossary terms consistent; each chapter has a summary + 3–5 study questions where applicable.

Day 11 — References and citations
- Check in‑text citations vs. reference list; verify key refs (publication years, journal, DOI) and mark missing DOIs.
- Use reference manager or a script to spot duplicates or missing entries.
Quality checks: all in‑text citations have matching refs; reference list formatted to style sheet.

Day 12 — Figures, tables, permissions, and accessibility
- Finalize figure captions and callouts; confirm resolution/format for production; collect final permissions or confirm they’re granted.
- Add alt text for figures and ensure color choices work for print and color‑blind accessibility.
Quality checks: all figures cleared or a permission request sent; alt text present; legends convey the take‑home message.

Day 13 — Copyedit / proofreading pass
- Single‑pass copyedit for punctuation, grammar, hyphenation, and style conformity. Read aloud key paragraphs to test rhythm.
- Resolve or log all remaining author queries; start compiling a change log.
Quality checks: no recurring grammar/style errors remain; author queries reduced to a final short list.

Day 14 — Final compile, index/TOC checks, and signoff
- Produce final compiled files (PDF/word as required), update TOC and running heads, perform a search for placeholders (TK, ???, XXX).
- Do a last quick read of chapter openings and endings to ensure the zoom out/zoom in links still make sense after edits.
- Send final pack to stakeholders with a concise change log and remaining items (if any).
Quality checks: clean compile with no placeholders; TOC and chapter numbers correct; deliverable and change log sent.

Day‑by‑day micro checklist (15–30 min at end of each day)
- Save versioned files with date and brief note.
- Update Author Queries log with any unresolved issues.
- Mark chapter tasks complete in your chapter map.
- Quick search for “TK”, “TODO”, “?” and citations lacking details.

Acceptance criteria for “finished” chapters
- Each chapter has a one‑line purpose, clear opening/closing linking statements, and a consistent pedagogical structure.
- Paragraphs present one idea each; dense passages simplified without loss of rigor (use light metaphors sparingly).
- All figures/tables are referenced and have clear captions; permissions requested/cleared.
- Reference list complete and formatted; glossary and notation consistent across chapters.
- Final compile contains no placeholders and is ready for production or author review.

Tools and habits to help
- Track Changes + a running Author Queries doc.
- A short, shareable style sheet (one page if possible) for quick reference.
- Timers and focused blocks (Pomodoro 25/50 min) to keep edits intense and consistent.
- Read‑aloud for final flow checks; automated grammar tools for catching obvious slips but don’t rely on them for content decisions.

answer:
Day-by-day plan (5-day week) plus the exact opening checklist and group safety‑pass card you can print/use.

Day 1 — Layout & zones
- Decide table layout and label clear workspace zones: “materials,” “messy/working,” and “finished/clean.” (Makes the room feel purposeful, less like a free‑for‑all.)
- Identify and mark the visible cleanup station(s): sink, waste bin(s), sharps/tray location.
- Print the Dissection Lab Opening Checklist and Group Safety Pass cards (text below).
- Gather trays for tool kits and sheathed scalpels (keep sheaths on until distribution).
- Collect goggles and gloves and stage them by table.

Day 2 — Station kits & visible routines
- Assemble each table’s tray: sheathed scalpel, spare sheath, forceps if used, paper towels, gloves, goggles, and the Group Safety Pass card.
- Cover specimens and stage them where students can’t touch until you’re ready (you’ll reveal them during the opening).
- Place a safety/cleanup reminder sign by the sink and waste bin (simple directions: sharps on tray, waste goes in bin, call teacher if unsure).
- Prepare a short demo script (use the script/checklist below verbatim).

Day 3 — Roles, scripts, and staff run‑through
- Decide simple group roles to suggest to students (materials gatherer, measurer, recorder). Keep roles informal but named.
- Train any assistants/TAs on the opening sequence:
  - Demo scalpel set‑down motion and have students practice with empty hands.
  - Enforce “tools only after goggles, gloves, and a clear workspace.”
  - Use the quick group check: “Show me how you set the scalpel down” / “Tell me where waste goes.”
  - Circulate and narrate during the lab (e.g., “I like how this group is checking measurements before mixing”) to nudge safe behavior without stopping class.
- Rehearse the minute‑by‑minute opening once as a team so everyone knows pacing.

Day 4 — Final prep & quick pilot
- Place trays and PPE at each table, leave specimens covered.
- Leave a Group Safety Pass card on each table.
- Walk the room and simulate the quick safety check at a few tables (verify trays have sheaths, gloves/goggles present, pass card visible).
- Confirm cleanup supplies and waste stations are accessible and clearly labeled.

Day 5 — Lab day: run the 15‑minute opening exactly
- Use the Dissection Lab Opening Checklist (below) as your script; hand out tool trays only after safety passes.
- Circulate and narrate; if spills/breaks happen, treat them as normal and fixable to keep tone calm.
- After groups return pass cards and receive tools, continue to circulate and reinforce cleanup rules (sharps stay on tray; anything dropped or uncertain = call teacher).

Printable Dissection Lab Opening Checklist (First 15 Minutes)
0–1 min
- Gather students at the front with specimens covered.
- Say: “We’re going to explore structures you’ve only seen in diagrams. First I’ll show you how we keep this exciting and safe.”

1–3 min
- Hold up a sheathed scalpel.
- Say: “This always points down, stays on the table when not in use, and only moves when everyone at your station knows where it’s going.”
- Demonstrate setting it down slowly with blade direction controlled.

3–4 min
- Have students mimic the set‑down motion with empty hands.

4–6 min
- Say: “You’ll get tools only after goggles are on, gloves are on, and your workspace is clear.”
- Point to the waste bin and sink.
- Say: “Sharps stay on the tray. Waste goes here. If anything drops or you’re unsure, call me over.”

6–10 min
- Visit each group for a quick safety check.
- Ask: “Show me how you set a scalpel down,” and “Tell me where waste goes.”
- If they demonstrate correctly, leave a safety‑pass card at their table.

10–12 min
- Uncover specimens.
- Say: “Tools appear only after I place them on your tray. If you’re gloved, goggled, and your space looks good, you’re ready.”

12–15 min
- Distribute tools to cleared groups.
- Answer quick questions, confirm calm tone, begin the lab.

Group Safety Pass Card (place on each table)
Your group gets tools after showing all three:
• Demonstrate the safe “set‑down” motion.
• Point to the correct waste location.
• Show that goggles, gloves, and a clear workspace are ready.
Hand this card back to the teacher to receive your tool tray.

Quick post‑lab reminders (use after the session)
- Ensure sharps remain on trays for collection.
- Direct waste to the marked bin and confirm students wash hands.
- Treat any spills/breaks as normal and fixable; model calm cleanup.

Overview assumptions

Day 1 — Confirm & order (2–3 hours)

Tasks/checklist:

- Confirm number of groups, student roster, partners. [Resp: you]
- Inventory existing supplies: dissection kits (scalpels with sheaths, scissors, forceps, probes, pins, trays), goggles, nitrile gloves (S/M/L), aprons, sharps containers, biohazard bags, disinfectant, paper towels, soap. Mark shortages. [Resp: lab tech/you]
- Order/repurchase missing PPE, extra scalpel blades/sheaths, sharps containers, specimen fixative/storage supplies, replacement tools. Note lead time. [Resp: you/lab admin]
- Reserve sinks, prep room, refrigerator or fixative storage if needed. [Resp: you/admin]
- Print safety forms, Group Safety Pass cards, signage templates. [Resp: you/admin]
- Schedule TA/assistant training session (Day 3). [Resp: you]

Day 2 — Kit assembly & station planning (2–4 hours)
Goals: assemble one complete kit per group, design station layout, prepare demo/training items.
Tasks/checklist:
- Assemble N complete dissection kits (N = #groups + 1 spare). Include sealed scalpel sheathed, scissors, forceps, probe, tray, pins, paper towel, waste bag. Label trays by group number. [Resp: lab tech/volunteers]
- Prepare a teacher demo kit and scalpel trainer (blunted trainer or wooden stylus). [Resp: you]
- Print and cut Group Safety Pass cards; print quick instruction sheets for each station (one per group). [Resp: admin]
- Create station map: mark “clean zone” (tool tray), “messy zone” (specimen), “used-waste” zone, and “traffic/teacher access” path. Tape zones to tables. [Resp: you]
- Prepare sharps containers and place temporary holding points for full containers. [Resp: lab tech]
- Create a one-page “teacher script” for the first 10–15 minutes (use earlier script/checklist). [Resp: you]
- Check inventory counts and update order list if anything still missing. [Resp: you]

Day 3 — Safety rehearsal & TA training (1.5–2 hours)
Goals: make TAs confident delivering the opening, supervising, and handling incidents.
Tasks/checklist:
- TA training (45–60 min): walk through your 10–15 min opening, demonstrate safe set‑down and scalpel pass, review waste protocol, sharps handling, and how to use Safety Pass card. Role-play student questions and a dropped scalpel scenario. [Resp: you]
- Have each TA practice the “set‑down” motion and scalpel pass using trainer; verify competency. [Resp: TAs]
- Assign TA stations and responsibilities: who monitors which stations, who handles sharps, who logs incidents. Post these assignments on the whiteboard. [Resp: you]
- Prepare incident log sheet, sharps disposal log, and emergency contacts (nurse, custodian, admin). [Resp: admin]
- Run a timed dry‑run of opening sequence with TAs and 1–2 volunteer students (10–15 min) to check flow and timing. Adjust script if needed. [Resp: you/TAs]

Day 4 — Physical setup & final prep (2–3 hours)
Goals: arrange tables, place trays, set up cleaning and disposal stations, signage, and final inventory.
Tasks/checklist:
- Physically arrange lab layout per Day 2 map: place trays, label group numbers, place goggles & gloves at each station (or box for students to pick sizes). [Resp: lab tech/TAs]
- Set up cleanup station: disinfectant, paper towels, sink access, labeled biohazard/waste bins, sharps container(s) at central pickup point. [Resp: lab tech]
- Post signage: PPE required, emergency procedures, step-by-step waste routing, teacher/TA locations. [Resp: you/admin]
- Test sinks, water flow, and paper towel/soap supply. [Resp: lab tech]
- Place demo station and teacher script at front; ensure overhead camera or close-up demo kit works if you plan a live demo. [Resp: you/AV]
- Do a final tool and PPE count vs. expected. Charge extra gloves and spare tools. [Resp: lab tech]
- Prepare student handouts/prelab quiz and email/forms to students (consent forms if required). [Resp: you/admin]

Day 5 — Lab day: final checks & execution (90–120 min prep before class)
Goals: confirm specimens and stations ready, run opening 10–15 min safety routine, supervise lab, and ensure post‑lab cleanup.
Morning pre-class checklist (30–60 min before students arrive):
- Verify specimens are prepped and stored correctly; bring to room only when ready. [Resp: you/lab tech]
- Confirm all trays have full kits and are placed at assigned stations. [Resp: TAs]
- Place Group Safety Pass card on each table (one per group). [Resp: TAs]
- Confirm sharps container(s) present, labeled, and accessible. [Resp: TAs]
- Confirm goggles & gloves available in sizes; post “no gloves = no tools” sign. [Resp: TAs]
- Place one demo scalpel (sheathed) and trainer at front; run last quick demo. [Resp: you]
- Remind TAs of their lines of sight and escalation protocol. [Resp: you/TAs]

First 15 minutes (use printed script; ~as in earlier checklist)
- 0–1 min: Gather class with specimens covered; opener to create curiosity.
- 1–3 min: Show sheathed scalpel; demonstrate set‑down.
- 3–4 min: Students mimic motion with empty hands.
- 4–6 min: Explain goggles/gloves/cleanup/waste rules; point to bins and sink.
- 6–10 min: Walk table-to-table for quick check: “Show me set‑down” and “Where does waste go?” Leave Group Safety Pass if they pass.
- 10–12 min: Uncover specimens and remind that tools only come after teacher places tray.
- 12–15 min: Distribute tool trays to cleared groups; begin work.

During lab:
- TAs circulate; one TA per 2–3 groups if possible. Enforce “no tool use until safety pass given.”
- Use incident log if any mishap; move student to nurse/call admin as needed.
- Encourage calm narration and redirecting groups that rush.

Post‑lab cleanup (20–30 min)
- Students follow posted cleanup: remove gloves, put waste in biohazard bags, place sharps in container, disinfect tray and table. TAs verify.
- Collect completed Group Safety Pass cards (optional for record).
- Log sharps container fullness and arrange disposal pickup if needed.
- Quick debrief: 5 min to review what went well and any safety notes for next session.

Ready‑to‑print Group Safety Pass (put one on each table)
Your group gets tools after showing all three:
• Demonstrate the safe “set‑down” motion.  
• Point to the correct waste location.  
• Show that goggles, gloves, and a clear workspace are ready.  
Hand this card back to the teacher to receive your tool tray.

Quick materials checklist (per group)
- Dissection tray + specimen (or specimen assignment per group)
- Dissection kit: sheathed scalpel, scissors, forceps, probe, pins
- Goggles (1 per student), nitrile gloves (various sizes), apron
- Paper towels, disinfectant wipes, waste bag
- Group Safety Pass card, quick instructions sheet
- Spare blade sheaths and spare gloves stored centrally

Contingency notes (brief)
- Missing PPE: postpone scalpel distribution; do anatomy demo or have students do observation/writing tasks while waiting.
- Late specimens: run prelab discussion, video demo, or practice tool-handling with trainers.
- Noncompliance: remove tool access, give short remediation, document incidents.
